images.caption: Figure 1:Overview of Neuro-VL training data, workflow, and evaluation.a, We curated the largest neuroimaging dataset to date, containing nearly 1 million studies collected from 450,000 patients, comprising 10 million volumetric scans. The dataset captures the full spectrum of neurological pathology, including neoplastic, vascular, infectious, degenerative, traumatic, and other conditions.b, Neuro-VL was trained to generate robust radiological interpretations of neuroimaging accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace. To reason over image and language input, Neuro-VL integrates a visual encoder with an LLM through a vision-language connector (not shown). The visual encoder incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism inspired by the inherent structure of neuroimaging data and is pretrained using radiology reports, enabling it to extract semantically rich visual features from complex neuroimaging studies.c, We evaluated Neuro-VL across internal health-system cohorts and 24 international public datasets spanning 21 countries. This evaluation covered diverse tasks, including localization, feature description, diagnosis, report generation, and longitudinal disease monitoring, as well as a comprehensive red-teaming evaluation.

Figure 2:Neuro-VL results.a, Overview of benchmark questions across source datasets and diagnostic categories. We curated neuroimaging studies from both an internal held-out test set and 24 international public datasets, forming 7 evaluation groups encompassing a broad spectrum of neurological pathologies.b, Closed-ended question-answering performance across 17 task-groups (n=31,975 in total), compared with the frontier model GPT-5.4 (OpenAI), the leading open-weight model Gemma 4 (Google DeepMind), and the leading neuroradiology-specialized model NeuroVFM. Results are accuracy, except for Open-Brain-20 feature description and CQ500/RSNA diagnosis, which use balanced accuracy.c, Radiology report generation performance across the internal held-out test set and two public datasets (n=3,933 in total). Results are proportions of pairwise preferences relative to the reference radiologist report as determined by NeuroJudge, an expert-validated LLM-based evaluator.d, Neuro-VL interpreting a complex head CT from the RSNA dataset, showing acute subarachnoid hemorrhage following rupture of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm and subsequent craniotomy for aneurysm clipping.e, Neuro-VL interpreting a brain MRI study from the BraTS dataset, showing a large heterogeneous left frontal mass with extensive vasogenic edema, mass effect, rightward midline shift, subfalcine herniation, and ventricular dilation.
In bothdande, Neuro-VL correctly localizes, describes, and diagnoses all significant findings while demonstrating grounded text-to-vision attention to each pathological finding. Additionally, the responses demonstrate Neuro-VL’s ability to engage in multi-turn conversations and perform contextual clinical reasoning.

Figure 3:Neuro-VL for longitudinal disease monitoring.a, Schematic of longitudinal neuroimaging interpretation for disease monitoring. Neuro-VL can integrate imaging findings across multiple time points to assess tumor recurrence following treatment.b,Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal, GPT-5.4, and Gemma 4 on change characterization (n=718), disease trajectory assessment (n=710), and intervention characterization (n=132). Results are mean accuracy with 95% CIs.PPvalues compare Neuro-VL with the highest-scoring comparator.c,Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal compared with GPT-5.4 and Gemma 4 on longitudinal report generation (n=734). Results are proportions of pairwise preferences relative to the reference radiologist report as determined by NeuroJudge, an expert-validated LLM-based evaluator.d, Neuro-VL interpreting a pair of brain MRI studies acquired 6 months apart. Neuro-VL identifies disease progression characterized by increased tumor burden, new nodular enhancement, extensive surrounding edema, and new mass effect with midline shift.

Figure 4:Red-teaming Neuro-VL with misleading prompts and clinical context.a,Schematic of thefabrication resistanceevaluation, comparing a neutral request with one assuming a pathology is present on a normal study.b,Fabrication resistance performance in normal studies (n=320), comparing neutral wording, pathology assumed, and pathology plus location assumed. Results are success rate over the evaluation set, where success requires avoiding significant pathology assertions throughout the answer.c,Schematic of themisdiagnosis resistanceevaluation, comparing prompts that provide the correct diagnosis (concordant) with those that provide an incorrect alternative (discordant). For themislocalization resistanceevaluation (not shown), prompts providing a concordant location are compared with those providing a discordant location, without specifying a diagnosis.d,Misdiagnosis resistance (left) and mislocalization resistance (right) performance on studies (n=246) with expert-annotated glioma or infarct. Results are success rate over the evaluation set, where success requires an interpretation compatible with the true lesion diagnosis or lesion location, respectively.
Forbandd, error bars indicate 95% CIs, andPPvalues compare the highest bar and second-highest bars within each group.

Extended Data Figure 1:Health system neuroimaging dataset.a,Dataset curation and partitioning. We queried the Michigan Medicine picture archiving and communication system (PACS) for MRI and CT studies of the head, brain, face, orbits, and neck. Of 961,683 curated studies, we held out 24,360 acquired on or after 1 July 2025 and 25,817 earlier studies from the same patients to prevent patient overlap with the training set. This yielded 911,506 training studies and 50,177 held-out studies, of which we reserved 1,552 for validation and 48,625 for testing.b,Example neuroimaging study. Astudycontains one or morescans, which may differ in imaging parameters or anatomical coverage. Radiologists interpret these scans together.c,Training set composition by modality and scan type. The training set comprised 392,236 MRI studies (5,434,754 scans) and 519,270 CT studies (3,644,581 scans), totaling 9,079,335 scans.d,Geographic distribution of studies by state of acquisition. The dataset included studies acquired at external imaging centers and transferred to Michigan Medicine for continuity of care.e–h,Distribution ofe,imaged anatomical region by scan;f,scanner manufacturer by study;g,examination year by study, stratified by modality; andh,patient age by study, stratified by sex.i,Extraction of diagnostic labels from radiology reports. We used a previously described LLM pipeline[4]to extract labels spanning 74 MRI and 82 CT diagnostic categories.j,Counts of diagnostic labels grouped into 11 broader diagnostic categories, stratified by modality. A study may contribute labels to multiple categories.

Extended Data Figure 2:Neuro-VL architecture and pretraining.a,Hierarchical organization and patch tokenization of a neuroimaging study, illustrated with MRI scans. The visual encoder projects each6×16×166\times 16\times 16voxel patch into a token and groups tokens at three levels: adjacent slices, individual scans, and the entire study. This process leverages the intrinsic data hierarchy of clinical radiology data.b,Visual encoder architecture and dual contrastive pretraining. We adapted the hierarchical attention mechanism from HLIP[2]to a 24-layer ViT-Large backbone. The encoder comprises four blocks, each containing four slice-attention layers, one scan-attention layer, and one study-attention layer, applied sequentially. Each layer computes self-attention within the corresponding token groups. The encoder learned semantically rich neuroimaging visual representations through language-image pretraining with a novel dual-contrastive objective. We introduced two learnable visual tokens to capture focal features from individual findings and holistic features from the entire study. Separate contrastive losses aligned these features with a randomly sampled sentence and the full report summary, respectively. We generated report summaries using a previously described LLM pipeline[4].c,Zero-shot classification performance of the Neuro-VL visual encoder, HLIP, and BiomedCLIP[23]on MR-RATE[27](brain MRI), CQ500[49](head CT), and RSNA[50](head CT). Results are macro-average AUROC with 95% CIs and brackets identify the comparisons with displayedPPvalues. Gray points show performance on individual diagnostic labels in RSNA and CQ500.d,Neuro-VL combines the visual encoder, a vision-language connector, and the Qwen3-8B language model[24]. The model generates responses conditioned on the input scans and user instruction.e,The vision-language connector concatenates each2×22\times 2group of adjacent visual tokens within a slice, reducing the token count fourfold. A two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) then projects the merged features into the language model’s embedding space.

Extended Data Figure 3:Visual instruction tuning data development.a–c,Three milestones in our iterative, expert-guided generation of the Neuro-VL visual instruction tuning dataset.a,We initially used the GPT-5 family of models[15]to generate clinically relevant questions and answers from radiology reports. After each training round, evaluators with neuroradiology expertise interacted with Neuro-VL on a validation set distinct from the held-out test set. Their feedback guided revisions to the data-generation strategy and subsequent retraining. Panelsbandchighlight two key refinements.b,During validation interactions, evaluators observed improved generalizability after training with avisual reasoning trace. We trained Neuro-VL to first describe visual findings grounded in the input scans (visual assessment) and then apply neuroradiology knowledge (reasoning) to synthesize the final answer. The curves show substantially lower negative log-likelihood training loss with visual reasoning supervision than with answer-only supervision.c,During subsequent review, evaluators identified a problem with fabricated scan references: the model sometimes described findings on scan types absent from the input, such as diffusion-weighted images when no such scans were provided. To address this, we incorporated imaging metadata, including modality, scan type, anatomical coverage, orientation, and radiologist-reported image quality, into the training targets as animaging statementpreceding the visual reasoning trace and final answer. Training loss decreased further with this strategy.
Extended Data Fig.7e compares Neuro-VL with Neuro-VL-Instant, which omits both intermediate components, and separately evaluates scan-reference faithfulness with and without imaging statements.d–f,Statistical overview of the final visual instruction tuning dataset.d,Distribution of training example topics. The dataset comprised approximately 740,000 examples spanning six main topics and additional clinically relevant topics, such as triage, critical finding rule-out, and specific region inspection, grouped under “Other.”e,Text and visual token composition of the training dataset, totaling approximately 2.3 billion tokens.f,Text token-count distributions for imaging statements, visual reasoning traces, and answers across all instruction examples.

Extended Data Figure 7:Neuro-VL subgroup and ablation analyses.a–d,Performance of Neuro-VL, GPT-5.4[17], and Gemma 4[18]by diagnostic category and demographic group in the Internal MRI and Internal CT benchmarks. Analysis pooled localization, feature description, and diagnosis questions within each cohort.a,d,Accuracy by diagnostic category in Internal MRI (a) and Internal CT (d). Categories correspond to the pathology of interest in each question.b,c,Age- and sex-related accuracy gaps in Internal MRI (b) and Internal CT (c). Bars show pediatric (age<18<18years) minus adult (age⩾18\geqslant 18years) accuracy on the left and female minus male accuracy on the right. Negative values indicate lower accuracy in the pediatric or female group, respectively.e,Evaluation of visual reasoning traces and imaging statements. The left plot compares Neuro-VL with Neuro-VL-Instant on Open-Brain-20. Neuro-VL-Instant generates answers directly, without either intermediate component. The right plot compares scan-reference faithfulness of Neuro-VL and a variant trained without imaging statements on CQ500, MR-RATE, and Open-Brain-20. Scan-reference faithfulness measures whether the visual reasoning trace refers only to scan types present in the input.f,Effect of clinical indication on Neuro-VL report generation on Internal MRI and Internal CT. Stacked bars show the proportions of NeuroJudge comparisons favoring reports generated with clinical indication, ties, and comparisons favoring reports generated without clinical indication. The dashed line marks 50%.g,Performance of the full generative Neuro-VL model vs. its CLIP-pretrained visual encoder alone on Open-Brain-20.
Error bars show 95% CIs. Brackets ineandgidentify the comparisons with displayedPPvalues. Gray points for the Open-Brain-20 results indicate performance on individual constituent datasets.

Extended Data Figure 8:Neuro-VL-Longitudinal training and evaluation.a,Example longitudinal imaging of a left caudothalamic mass, with prior brain MRI and follow-up CT six years later showing enlargement with hemorrhage.b,Generation of longitudinal visual instruction tuning data. We used the GPT-5 family of models[15]to generate clinically relevant questions, imaging statements, visual reasoning traces, and answers from paired prior and current radiology reports and imaging metadata.c,Distribution of training example topics in the longitudinal training dataset, comprising approximately 230,000 examples in total.d,Text and visual token composition of the longitudinal training dataset, totaling approximately 1.3 billion tokens.e,Text token-count distributions for imaging statements, visual reasoning traces, and answers across all longitudinal instruction examples.f,Comparison of Neuro-VL and Neuro-VL-Longitudinal on matched questions. Bars show equally weighted mean performance across 17 single-study tasks and, separately, three longitudinal tasks.g,Lesion-size estimation on BraTS glioma and meningioma MRI studies[29,30]. Points compare each study’s segmentation-derived reference dimensions with the mean measurement from five temperature-sampled Neuro-VL responses across three dimensions: anteroposterior (AP), transverse (LR), and craniocaudal (SI). Mean absolute error (MAE) averages absolute errors across generations within each study and then equally across studies.h–j,Accuracy in the internal longitudinal benchmark stratified byh,pathology interval change type,i,time between studies, andj,clinical follow-up scenario. Bars compare Neuro-VL-Longitudinal, GPT-5.4[17], and Gemma 4[18], pooling change-characterization and disease-trajectory-assessment questions.
Error bars infandh–jshow 95% CIs. Brackets identify the comparisons with displayedPPvalues.
